title: Asking Team Members to Express What the Organization Means to Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article suggests a simple but underused leadership practice: periodically asking team members, in a group setting, what the organization actually means to them. Because leaders mostly hear complaints and handle HR issues, they tend to underestimate how much people value the mission and culture — until they directly ask. The piece is specific about framing: asking 'what does the organization mean to you' works better than asking what people like or how they benefit, which tends to invite mixed or negative answers. It recommends this as a short, 10-15 minute closing exercise at offsites or team gatherings that leaves people with a stronger shared appreciation for the team.
points: Leaders often underestimate how much the organization means to committed team members.
Asking people directly to share their feelings about the organization surfaces this underappreciated sentiment.
The specific framing matters — 'what does it mean to you' works better than 'what do you like' or 'how does it benefit you.'
The exercise takes only 10-15 minutes and fits naturally at the end of offsites or team gatherings.
Hearing colleagues speak positively about the organization has a ripple effect on less-engaged team members.
quotes: Leaders are often surprised by how much the organization or team means to team members.
Because they hear so many complaints and field so many human resources issues, leaders often think the value of the organization is underappreciated or taken for granted.
Leaders are often surprised at how deeply and positively team members feel about the team and organization.
Leaders who ask the question: “What does the team and organization mean to you?” will get the ball rolling.
Framing the question about value and meaning exclusively will normally solicit an upswell of thoughtful and heartfelt comments.
